opus-5.5.text:
I think the core problem is that current capabilities are a very misleading guide to what's actually going to matter economically. When people look at today's systems, they see the specific things these models happen to be good at, like writing code snippets, answering questions, or summarizing documents, and they project forward by imagining a somewhat better version of the same thing. But the most valuable applications of a technology usually don't look like a slightly improved version of its first applications.

Think about electricity or computers. If you'd looked at early computers and asked what they were good for, you'd have said ballistics tables and code-breaking. Extrapolating from that wouldn't have gotten you to the internet or to software reorganizing nearly every industry. The big impact came once the technology became general and cheap enough to be woven into everything, and that's very hard to see from the early use cases.

There's also a subtler issue with AI specifically. The capabilities we have now are quite uneven. Models are surprisingly strong at things we used to think were hard, like reasoning through competition math or writing fluent prose, and surprisingly weak at things that seem easy to us: sustained agency over long tasks, reliably operating in messy real-world environments, coordinating with people over weeks, or remembering and learning on the job. Most of the economy runs on that second category. A large share of work isn't about solving a crisp, self-contained problem. It's about handling a long sequence of small, context-dependent decisions without supervision.

So if you extrapolate from what's impressive today, you end up overestimating how quickly AI will transform areas that look like benchmarks, and you underestimate how transformative it will be once those less glamorous capabilities like agency, reliability, and adaptation get solved. When that happens, I don't expect AI to just be a better chatbot or coding assistant. I expect it to be able to substitute for human labor much more broadly, and that's a qualitatively different world, not a smooth continuation of the current trend line in product features.

The better way to think about it, in my view, is to ask what bottlenecks remain between current systems and being able to do most of the tasks humans do, and how fast compute, algorithms, and data are likely to close those gaps. That gives you a much more useful picture than asking which of today's demos will get better.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core problem is that when people extrapolate, they're usually extrapolating along the wrong axis. They look at what current systems can do, imagine a slightly better version of that, and then ask how that version would slot into the economy as it exists today. But that's not how transformative technologies have historically played out.

Take electricity, or computers more broadly. If you'd asked someone in the 1950s what computers would be used for, they'd have described faster versions of the tasks they were already doing by hand: ballistics calculations, census tabulation, payroll. Almost nobody predicted that the dominant uses would end up being things like social networks, video streaming, or search engines, because those applications only make sense once the technology is cheap enough and widespread enough that entirely new workflows get built around it. The applications aren't a function of the capability alone. They're a function of the capability plus all the complementary investments, organizational changes, and cost reductions that happen downstream.

So with AI, I think the mistake is to look at a language model today, notice that it's good at writing emails and summarizing documents and writing some code, and conclude that the future is basically "better email writing." The actually important question is what becomes possible when you have something that can do most cognitive labor at a tiny fraction of the cost of a human, and you can spin up millions of copies in parallel. That's a regime where the bottlenecks shift entirely. The constraint stops being "can the model do this task" and becomes things like compute, energy, physical infrastructure, regulatory friction, and how fast organizations can restructure themselves.

There's also a more subtle issue, which is that current benchmarks and demos tell you about performance on tasks we already know how to specify. But a lot of the economic value in the world comes from long-horizon, messy, poorly specified work, where the hard part is figuring out what to do rather than executing a well-defined step. Current systems are pretty uneven there, and I'd expect the capabilities that close that gap to look different in kind, not just degree. So naive extrapolation of benchmark trends gives you a misleading picture both of what the systems will be good at and of what people will end up using them for.

My preferred approach is to think less about specific applications and more about aggregate economic dynamics: how much of total labor is substitutable, how quickly costs fall, how fast capital can be redeployed. Those are the variables that actually determine the trajectory, and they're much more robust to being wrong about the details of which particular use case takes off.

astra-6.text:
I think the main problem is that what you see AI being used for today is the result of both its capabilities and the effort people have put into figuring out how to use it. And those things evolve on different timescales. You can get a more capable model quite quickly, but reorganizing a business around that model, building the complementary software, and figuring out which applications are actually valuable can take much longer.

So even if capabilities stopped improving, I would expect applications to keep expanding for quite a while. We haven't necessarily discovered all the useful things you can do with existing systems.

The other issue is that applications can depend on crossing a threshold. A system that can do most of a task, but needs someone to check it constantly, might not be particularly useful. Once it becomes reliable enough that you can delegate the task, the economics can change quite sharply. A relatively smooth improvement in capability can therefore produce a much larger change in what people use the system for.

That makes extrapolating from current use misleading. You're looking at systems that are still improving, through an adoption process that is itself lagging behind them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main problem is that what an AI system can do today is only a snapshot, and applications often depend on crossing a threshold. You can have a system that’s quite impressive at a task but still not reliable enough to use economically. Then a relatively small improvement in capability can make the whole application viable. If you extrapolate from how people are using the earlier system, you can miss that transition.

Software engineering is a useful example. A system that can write a short function is helpful, but someone still has to specify the task, check the output, and integrate it. If the system can instead handle a substantial project with less supervision, the economics look very different. It’s not just a proportionate increase in the value of autocomplete.

There’s also adaptation on the other side. People build tools, change workflows, and reorganize work around what the systems can do. Those changes take time, so current applications don’t even reveal all the possibilities of current capabilities, let alone future ones.

So I’d distinguish predicting improvements in capabilities from predicting the applications those improvements will produce. Even if the first follows a fairly smooth trend, the second can be much more discontinuous.
